insurrection

in-suh-REK-shun -- shares a root with 'resurrect,' meaning to rise. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Insurrection is a violent uprising against an established authority.

Soldiers were called in overnight after an armed insurrection broke out near the capitol steps.

Example

A group of angry factory workers seizes control of the building overnight, blocking every entrance and demanding the owner be removed by force.

That organized, violent rising-up against authority is exactly what an insurrection is. Unlike 'protest,' which can be entirely peaceful, insurrection specifically implies force and open rebellion.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rebellion: A rebellion is organized resistance against authority, and it can smolder for months or years, sometimes without open violence. An insurrection is more compressed and always violent: a sudden, armed rising against established power, often over in days.

revolt: A revolt is the broad, everyday word for turning against a ruler or authority, and it stretches to small or even bloodless refusals, like a boardroom revolt. An insurrection is narrower: the formal, legal term for a violent, organized rising -- the word used in criminal charges.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

compliance: obedience to rules or authority

submission: the act of yielding to another's authority

Where it sits · how organized and armed the defiance is — uprising → insurrection → revolution

uprising vs. insurrection: An uprising is milder and looser than an insurrection -- any mass rising against those in power counts as an uprising, even an unarmed one, while an insurrection is an organized, armed attempt to defy authority.

revolution vs. insurrection: A revolution goes further than an insurrection: an insurrection is a violent strike against the people in power, while a revolution overturns the entire system of power and replaces it with a new one.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: against, upon (Latin)

Root — surrect

Root — surrect: to rise (from Latin surgere, 'to rise'; surrectus is its past form, as in resurrect)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or process of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('against, upon') + surrect ('to rise' — from Latin surgere, whose past form surrectus appears in resurrect) + -ion ('act or process of'): Latin insurgere meant 'to rise up against.' An insurrection, at its root, is a rising-up against authority — the same root that gives us resurrect and surge.

Use the root in a new word: resurrect

Use the root in a new word: resurrect: The old bakery on Main Street was resurrected by a new owner who kept every original recipe.
